items.stem: Amit is trying to rearrange his bedroom on a Sunday afternoon. First, he pushes a heavy vintage wooden wardrobe with a force of 150 N, but the wardrobe stubbornly refuses to move. Frustrated, he shifts his attention and pushes a lighter study chair with a 50 N force, successfully moving it by 2 metres across the floor in a straight line. Later, he lifts a 5 kg pile of heavy encyclopaedias and holds them perfectly steady on his head for three minutes while deciding where to place them on the shelf. Finally, balancing the books on his head, he walks horizontally across the room to reach the bookshelf. QUESTIONS: (a) How much work is done by Amit when he applies a 150 N force to push the heavy wooden wardrobe? (b) Calculate the work done by Amit on the study chair. (c) Explain why Amit does zero work while holding the heavy pile of books steady on his head, even though he might feel tired. (d) State the amount of work done by Amit against gravity when he walks horizontally across the room with the books on his head. Justify your answer.
items.answer: (a) The work done by Amit is zero because the displacement of the heavy wooden wardrobe is zero. (b) Work done on the chair = Force × displacement. = 50 N × 2 m = 100 J. (c) Amit does zero work on the books while holding them steady because there is no displacement. He feels tired because his muscles continuously consume internal bodily energy to maintain the upward force balancing gravity. (d) The work done against gravity is zero. This is because the gravitational force acts downwards, while Amit’s displacement is horizontal. Since the force and displacement Work, Energy, and Simple Machines are perpendicular to each other, no work is done by that force. 178. A student, Rohan, spends 10 minutes pushing against a stationary brick wall with all his might. He feels very tired afterwards and believes he has done a lot of work. However, the wall does not move at all. 1. According to the scientific definition of work, has Rohan done any work on the wall? Explain why or why not. 2. What two conditions must be satisfied for work to be done on an object? 3. Even though no scientific work was done on the wall, Rohan felt tired. Where did the energy he expended go?

items.stem: If Rohan had pushed a small toy car with the same force and it moved a distance of 2 meters, would work have been done on the toy car?
items.answer: 1. No, according to the scientific definition of work, Rohan has not done any work on the wall. Work is done when a force causes displacement of an object in the direction of the force. Since the wall did not move (no displacement), no work was done on it. 2. The two conditions are: (i) a force should act on an object, and (ii) the object must be displaced. 3. The energy Rohan expended was converted into heat within his own body due to muscular effort (internal energy changes, metabolic processes). 4. Yes, if Rohan pushed a toy car and it moved, work would have been done on the toy car because there was a force applied and a displacement in the direction of the force.

items.stem: During a crucial inter-school football tournament, Rahul, a star striker, receives a pass near the penalty area. He aggressively kicks the stationary ball straight towards the opponent’s goalpost. The ball speeds up rapidly and moves in the exact direction of his powerful kick. Seeing the impending danger, the opposing goalkeeper, Kabir, anticipates the trajectory. He dives elegantly and applies a strong force with his extended hands to stop the ball from entering the net. The momentum of the ball pushes Kabir’s hands slightly backward by 0.2 metres before the ball finally comes to a complete halt in his firm grip. QUESTIONS: (a) State the type of work done by Rahul when he kicks the stationary football. (b) Explain why the work done by the goalkeeper, Kabir, on the moving ball is considered negative work. (c) If Kabir applied a stopping force of 250 N and his hands moved back by 0.2 m in the direction of the ball’s motion, calculate the work done by him on the ball.
items.answer: (a) Rahul does positive work on the football because the force he applies and the resulting displacement of the ball are in the same direction. (b) Kabir applies a force in the opposite direction to the ball’s motion to stop it. When the applied force and the displacement of the object are in opposite directions, the work done is negative. (c) Work done = Force × displacement in the direction of force. Since Kabir’s force is opposite to the displacement, W = 250 N × (-0.2 m) = -50 J.

items.stem: In a spacious physics laboratory, a group of students is studying the principles of motion using two battery-operated toy cars, labeled Car A and Car B. Car A has a mass of 2 kg, while Car B is considerably heavier, with a mass of 4 kg. Initially, both cars are programmed to move side-by-side on a straight racing track at a constant velocity of 3 m/s. After recording their initial observations, the students modify the settings to increase the speed of Car A from 3 m/s to 6 m/s to investigate how a change in velocity mathematically impacts the energy possessed by a moving vehicle. Click Here to Buy book on Amazon QUESTIONS: (a) Define the term kinetic energy based on your understanding of the chapter. (b) While both cars are moving at the initial velocity of 3 m/s, which car possesses more kinetic energy? Give a reason for your choice. (c) Calculate how many times the kinetic energy of Car A increases when its velocity is doubled from 3 m/s to 6 m/s. Show your reasoning.
items.answer: (a) Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by an object due to its motion. (b) Car B possesses more kinetic energy. Since kinetic energy is directly proportional to mass (K = 1/2 mv2), for objects moving at the same velocity, the object with the greater mass will have higher kinetic energy. (c) The kinetic energy increases by 4 times. Kinetic energy is directly proportional to the square of the velocity (v2). When the velocity is doubled (2v), the square of the velocity becomes (2v)2 = 4v2, thus making the new kinetic energy four times the original value. 181. items.stem: Neha visits a local archery training centre during her summer vacation. She keenly observes an expert trainer demonstrating the correct technique to shoot an arrow. The trainer pulls the string of the flexible bow tightly backward, significantly changing its shape. He holds it there motionless for a few seconds, carefully aiming at the bullseye. When he releases the string, the arrow shoots forward at an incredibly high speed. After the practice session concludes, the trainer picks up a dropped 0.05 kg arrow from the floor and places it securely back into a wall-mounted quiver located exactly 2 metres above the ground. QUESTIONS: (a) Name the specific type of energy stored in the bow when the string is pulled tightly backward. (b) How does the stretched bow acquire this stored energy? (c) Describe the energy transformation that takes place the moment the trainer releases the stretched bowstring. (d) Calculate the potential energy gained by the arrow when the trainer lifts it from the ground to the quiver. (Assume g = 10 m/s^2) Work, Energy, and Simple Machines (e) Differentiate between the type of potential energy in the stretched bow and the arrow placed high in the quiver.
items.answer: (a) Elastic potential energy is stored in the stretched bow. (b) The bow acquires this energy because the trainer does work on it by applying muscular force to deform its original shape. This work is stored internally as potential energy due to its new configuration. (c) When the string is released, the bow rapidly returns to its original shape. The stored elastic potential energy of the bow is transferred to the arrow, converting into kinetic energy, which causes the arrow to fly forward. (d) Gravitational Potential Energy = mgh = 0.05 kg × 10 m/s^2 × 2 m = 1 J. (e) The stretched bow possesses potential energy due to its deformed shape or configuration (elastic potential energy). In contrast, the arrow in the quiver possesses potential energy due to its elevated position or height relative to the surface of the Earth (gravitational potential energy). 183. An archer pulls back the string of a bow, placing an arrow against it. When the string is released, the arrow flies off at a high speed towards the target. 1. When the archer pulls back the bowstring, what kind of energy is stored in the stretched bow? 2. What happens to this stored energy when the bowstring is released? 3. What kind of energy does the arrow possess as it flies towards the target?

items.stem: If the archer stretches the bowstring further back (more displacement), how does this affect the energy stored and the subsequent speed of the arrow (assuming arrow mass is constant)?
items.answer: 1. When the archer pulls back the bowstring, potential energy (specifically, elastic potential energy) is stored in the stretched bow. 2. When the bowstring is released, the stored potential energy in the bow is converted into kinetic energy of the arrow. 3. As the arrow flies towards the target, it possesses kinetic energy due to its motion. 4. Stretching the bowstring further back increases the potential energy stored in the bow. This increased potential energy will be converted into greater kinetic energy for the arrow, resulting in a higher speed for the arrow.

items.stem: A group of friends visits an amusement park and stands in awe watching a massive steel roller coaster. The empty coaster cars are slowly mechanically pulled up a steep incline to the highest peak of the ride, Point X, which is situated exactly 50 metres above the ground. At this peak, the cars briefly pause before plunging rapidly down a terrifying steep drop to Point Y, located just 5 metres above the ground. As the cars speed through the bottom track at their maximum velocity, the riders experience a thrilling rush. (Assume air resistance and track friction are completely negligible for this scenario). QUESTIONS: (a) What is mechanical energy defined as? (b) At Point X, what is the primary form of mechanical energy possessed by the roller coaster cars? (c) Based on energy conversion, explain why the speed of the roller coaster increases drastically as it moves downwards from Point X to Point Y. (d) If friction and air resistance are completely ignored, what happens to the total mechanical energy of the coaster during the steep drop? State the principle that supports this.
items.answer: (a) Mechanical energy is defined as the sum of the kinetic energy and the potential energy of an object. (b) At Point X (the highest point where the cars briefly pause), the roller coaster possesses maximum gravitational potential energy and zero kinetic energy. (c) As the coaster cars drop, their height above the ground decreases, causing a loss in potential energy. This lost potential energy is continuously converted into kinetic energy, resulting in a drastic increase in the cars’ speed. (d) The total mechanical energy of the coaster remains constant throughout the drop. This is supported by the law of conservation of mechanical energy, which states that if no external forces like friction act on an object, the sum of its kinetic and potential energy stays constant. 185. items.stem: On Independence Day, the school principal proudly hoists the national flag in the main courtyard. A long, sturdy rope is attached to the flag, passing through a small, grooved wheel securely fixed at the very top of a tall metal flagpole. When the principal pulls the rope downwards, the flag moves upwards smoothly. Later that afternoon, construction workers at the school are seen using a similar grooved wheel system. However, their wheel is attached directly to a heavy load of bricks and moves vertically up and down along with the load, helping them lift materials with minimal effort. QUESTIONS: (a) What is the specific name of the simple machine fixed at the top of the school’s flagpole? (b) Does the fixed wheel at the top of the flagpole reduce the magnitude of force the principal needs to apply? Why is it used? (c) How does the simple machine used by the construction workers differ from the one used for the flagpole in terms of mechanical advantage?
items.answer: (a) The simple machine at the top of the flagpole is called a fixed pulley. (b) No, a fixed pulley does not reduce the required force; its mechanical advantage is 1. It is used because it provides convenience by changing the direction of the effort, allowing the principal to pull downwards to lift the flag upwards. Journey Inside the Atom CHAPTER 8 Journey Inside the Atom SSummar 1. Rediscovering the Roots of Atomic Theory 1. Acharya Kanada in ancient India suggested that dividing matter repeatedly leads to the smallest indivisible particles called parmanus. 2. His ideas are recorded in the Sanskrit text Vaisesika Sutras. 3. Combinations of parmanus form dyads and triads to create the entire material universe. 4. Greek philosophers Leucippus and Democritus also proposed similar indivisible particles called atomos. 5. The word atomos means indivisible in Greek. 6. John Dalton proposed his atomic theory in 1808 based on scientific experiments of his time. 7. Dalton stated that all matter is composed of indivisible building blocks called atoms that cannot be broken down further. 8. Dalton’s theory was the first scientific description of how matter is made. 2. A Short Historical Journey Through Atomic Models 1. Scientists believed atoms were the smallest indivisible units of matter until the late 19th century. 2. The discovery of radioactivity showed that atoms emit invisible energy and particles. 3. This phenomenon proved that atoms are composed of smaller subatomic particles. 4. J J Thomson studied the conduction of electric current through low pressure gases in 1897. 5. He used a glass vacuum tube with a negative cathode and a positive anode connected to a high voltage supply. 6. He observed rays moving from the cathode to the anode and called them cathode rays. 7. Cathode rays are streams of tiny negatively charged particles called electrons. 8. Electrons have a much smaller mass than atoms and are fundamental components of all elements. 9. The charge of an electron is taken as minus 1 for convention and convenience. 10. J J Thomson received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1906 for his discovery of the electron. 3. Electrical nature of matter Since very early times, electrical nature of matter is known from the experiments on the production of frictional electricity, e.g., when a comb is rubbed with dry hair and then brought near small pieces of paper, it attracts pieces of paper. As matter is composed of atoms, there is an indication of the presence of charge in an atom. 4. When the pressure of the gas inside the discharge tube was 1 atm, electric current did not flow between electrodes because gases as such are bad conductors of electricity.
